Where the statistic ''s''<sup>2</sup>/''m'' is not constant it has been recommended to use instead to regress Lloyd's index against ''am'' + ''bm''<sup>2</sup> where ''a'' and ''b'' are constants.<ref name=Ho1993>{{cite journal | last1 = Ho | first1 = CC | year = 1993 | title = Dispersion statistics and sample size estimates for ''Tetranychus kanzawai'' (Acari: Tetranychidae) on mulberry | journal = Environ Entomol | volume = 22 | pages = 21–25 | doi=10.1093/ee/22.1.21}}</ref>

The sample size (''n'') for a given degree of precision (''D'') for this regression is given by<ref name="Ho1993"/>

: <math> n = \left( \frac t D \right)^2 \left( \frac{ a + 1 } { m } + b - 1 \right)</math>

where ''a'' is the constant in this regression, ''b'' is the slope, ''m'' is the mean and ''t'' is the critical value of the t distribution.

Iwao has proposed a sequential sampling test based on this regression.<ref name=Iwao1975>{{cite journal | last1 = Iwao | first1 = S | year = 1975 | title = A new method of sequential sampling to classify populations relative to a critical density | journal = Res Popul Ecol | volume = 16 | issue = 2| pages = 281–28 | doi=10.1007/bf02511067| s2cid = 20662793 }}</ref> The upper and lower limits of this test are based on critical densities m<sub>c</sub> where control of a pest requires action to be taken.

: <math> N_u = im_c + t( i ( a + 1 ) m_c + ( b - 1 ) m_c^2 )^{1/2} </math>

: <math> N_l = im_c - t( i ( a + 1 ) m_c + ( b - 1 ) m_c^2 )^{1/2} </math>

where ''N''<sub>''u''</sub> and ''N''<sub>''l''</sub> are the upper and lower bounds respectively, ''a'' is the constant from the regression, ''b'' is the slope and ''i'' is the number of samples.

Kuno has proposed an alternative sequential stopping test also based on this regression.<ref name=Kuno1969>{{cite journal | last1 = Kuno | first1 = E | year = 1969 | title = A new method of sequential sampling to obtain the population estimates with a fixed level of precision | journal = Res. Popul. Ecol. | volume = 11 | issue = 2| pages = 127–136 | doi=10.1007/bf02936264| s2cid = 35594101 }}</ref>

: <math> T_n = \frac { a + 1 } { D^2 - \frac { b - 1 } n } </math>

where ''T''<sub>''n''</sub> is the total sample size, ''D'' is the degree of precision, ''n'' is the number of samples units, a is the constant and b is the slope from the regression respectively.

Kuno's test is subject to the condition that ''n'' ≥ (''b'' − 1) / ''D''<sup>2</sup>

Parrella and Jones have proposed an alternative but related stop line<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Parrella | first1 = MP | last2 = Jones | first2 = VP | year = 1985 | title = Yellow traps as monitoring tools for ''Liriomyza trifolii'' (Diptera: Agromyzidae) in chrysanthemum greenhouses | journal = J Econ Entomol | volume = 78 | pages = 53–56 | doi=10.1093/jee/78.1.53}}</ref>

: <math> T_n = \left( 1 - \frac n N \right) \frac {a + 1} { D^2 - \left( 1 - \frac n N \right) \frac {b - 1} n } </math>

where ''a'' and ''b'' are the parameters from the regression, ''N'' is the maximum number of sampled units and ''n'' is the individual sample size.

===Morisita's index of dispersion===

[[Masaaki Morisita]]'s index of dispersion ( ''I''<sub>''m''</sub> ) is the scaled probability that two points chosen at random from the whole population are in the same sample.<ref name=Morisita1959>{{cite journal | last1 = Morisita | first1 = M | year = 1959 | title = Measuring the dispersion and the analysis of distribution patterns | journal = Memoirs of the Faculty of Science, Kyushu University Series E. Biol | volume = 2 | pages = 215–235 }}</ref> Higher values indicate a more clumped distribution.

: <math> I_m = \frac { \sum x ( x - 1 ) } { n m ( m - 1 ) } </math>

An alternative formulation is

: <math> I_m = n \frac{ \sum x^2 - \sum x } { ( \sum x )^2 - \sum x } </math>

where ''n'' is the total sample size, ''m'' is the sample mean and ''x'' are the individual values with the sum taken over the whole sample.
It is also equal to

: <math> I_m = \frac { n \operatorname{IMC} } {nm - 1} </math>

where ''IMC'' is Lloyd's index of crowding.<ref name="Lloyd1967"/>

This index is relatively independent of the population density but is affected by the sample size. Values > 1 indicate clumping; values < 1 indicate a uniformity of distribution and a value of 1 indicates a random sample.

Morisita showed that the statistic<ref name="Morisita1959"/>

: <math> I_m \left( \sum x - 1 \right) + n - \sum x </math>

is distributed as a chi squared variable with ''n''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1 degrees of freedom.

An alternative significance test for this index has been developed for large samples.<ref name=Pedigo1994>Pedigo LP & Buntin GD (1994) Handbook of sampling methods for arthropods in agriculture. CRC Boca Raton FL</ref>

: <math> z = \frac { I_m - 1 } { 2 / (n m^2)} </math>

where ''m'' is the overall sample mean, ''n'' is the number of sample units and ''z'' is the normal distribution [[abscissa]]. Significance is tested by comparing the value of ''z'' against the values of the [[normal distribution]].

A function for its calculation is available in the statistical [[R language]] in the [https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/vegan/html/dispindmorisita.html vegan package].

Note, not to be confused with [[Morisita's overlap index]].

===Standardised Morisita's index===

Smith-Gill developed a statistic based on Morisita's index which is independent of both sample size and population density and bounded by −1 and +1. This statistic is calculated as follows<ref name=Smith-Gill1975>{{cite journal | last1 = Smith-Gill | first1 = SJ | year = 1975 | title = Cytophysiological basis of disruptive pigmentary patterns in the leopard frog ''Rana pipiens''. II. Wild type and mutant cell specific patterns | journal = J Morphol | volume = 146 | issue = 1| pages = 35–54 | doi=10.1002/jmor.1051460103| pmid = 1080207 | s2cid = 23780609 }}</ref>

First determine Morisita's index ( ''I''<sub>''d''</sub> ) in the usual fashion. Then let ''k'' be the number of units the population was sampled from. Calculate the two critical values

: <math> M_u = \frac { \chi^2_{0.975} - k + \sum x } { \sum x - 1 } </math>

: <math> M_c = \frac { \chi^2_{0.025} - k + \sum x } { \sum x - 1 } </math>

where χ<sup>2</sup> is the chi square value for ''n'' − 1 degrees of freedom at the 97.5% and 2.5% levels of confidence.

The standardised index ( ''I''<sub>''p''</sub> ) is then calculated from one of the formulae below.

When ''I''<sub>''d''</sub> ≥ ''M''<sub>''c''</sub> > 1

: <math> I_p = 0.5 + 0.5 \left( \frac { I_d - M_c } { k - M_c } \right) </math>

When ''M''<sub>''c''</sub> > ''I''<sub>''d''</sub> ≥ 1

: <math> I_p = 0.5 \left( \frac { I_d - 1 } { M_u - 1 } \right) </math>

When 1 > ''I''<sub>''d''</sub> ≥ ''M''<sub>''u''</sub>

: <math> I_p = -0.5 \left( \frac { I_d - 1 } { M_u - 1 } \right) </math>

When 1 > ''M''<sub>''u''</sub> > ''I''<sub>''d''</sub>

: <math> I_p = -0.5 + 0.5 \left( \frac { I_d - M_u } { M_u } \right) </math>

''I''<sub>''p''</sub> ranges between +1 and −1 with 95% confidence intervals of ±0.5. ''I''<sub>''p''</sub> has the value of 0 if the pattern is random; if the pattern is uniform, ''I''<sub>''p''</sub> < 0 and if the pattern shows aggregation, ''I''<sub>''p''</sub> > 0.

===Southwood's index of spatial aggregation===

Southwood's index of spatial aggregation (''k'') is defined as

: <math> \frac {1}{k} = \frac{m^*}{m} - 1 </math>

where ''m'' is the mean of the sample and ''m''* is Lloyd's index of crowding.<ref name=Southwood1978 />

===Fisher's index of dispersion===

Fisher's [[index of dispersion]]<ref name=Elliot1977b>Elliot JM (1977) Statistical analysis of samples of benthic invertebrates. Freshwater Biological Association. Ambleside</ref><ref name=Fisher1925>Fisher RA (1925) Statistical methods for research workers. Hafner, New York</ref> is

: <math> \mathrm{ID} = \frac{( n - 1 ) s^2 }{ m } </math>

This index may be used to test for over dispersion of the population. It is recommended that in applications n > 5<ref name=Hoel1943>{{cite journal | last1 = Hoel | first1 = P | year = 1943 | title = On the indices of dispersion | journal = Ann Math Statist | volume = 14 | issue = 2| page = 155 | doi=10.1214/aoms/1177731457| doi-access = free }}</ref> and that the sample total divided by the number of samples is > 3. In symbols

: <math> \frac { \sum x } { n } > 3 </math>

where ''x'' is an individual sample value. The expectation of the index is equal to ''n'' and it is distributed as the [[chi-square distribution]] with ''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 degrees of freedom when the population is Poisson distributed.<ref name=Hoel1943 /> It is equal to the scale parameter when the population obeys the [[gamma distribution]].

It can be applied both to the overall population and to the individual areas sampled individually. The use of this test on the individual sample areas should also include the use of a Bonferroni correction factor.

If the population obeys Taylor's law then

: <math> \mathrm{ ID } = ( n - 1 ) a m^{ b - 1 } </math>

===Index of cluster size===

The index of cluster size (''ICS'') was created by David and Moore.<ref name=David1954>{{cite journal | last1 = David | first1 = FN | last2 = Moore | first2 = PG | year = 1954 | title = Notes on contagious distributions in plant populations | journal = Annals of Botany| volume = 18 | pages = 47–53 | doi=10.1093/oxfordjournals.aob.a083381}}</ref> Under a random (Poisson) distribution ''ICS'' is expected to equal 0. Positive values indicate a clumped distribution; negative values indicate a uniform distribution.

: <math> \mathrm{ ICS } = \frac{s^2}{m - 1} </math>

where ''s''<sup>2</sup> is the variance and ''m'' is the mean.

If the population obeys Taylor's law

: <math> \mathrm{ ICS } = a m^{ b - 1 } - 1 </math>

The ''ICS'' is also equal to Katz's test statistic divided by ( ''n'' / 2 )<sup>1/2</sup> where ''n'' is the sample size. It is also related to Clapham's test statistic. It is also sometimes referred to as the clumping index.

===Green's index===

Green's index (''GI'') is a modification of the index of cluster size that is independent of ''n'' the number of sample units.<ref name=Green1966>{{cite journal | last1 = Green | first1 = RH | year = 1966 | title = Measurement of non-randomness in spatial distributions | journal = Res Pop Ecol | volume = 8 | pages = 1–7 | doi=10.1007/bf02524740| s2cid = 25039063 }}</ref>

: <math> C_x = \frac { s^2 / m - 1 } { nm - 1 } </math>

This index equals 0 if the distribution is random, 1 if it is maximally aggregated and −1 / ( ''nm'' − 1 ) if it is uniform.

The distribution of Green's index is not currently known so statistical tests have been difficult to devise for it.

If the population obeys Taylor's law

: <math> C_x = \frac { a m^{ b - 1 } - 1 } {nm - 1}</math>

===Binary dispersal index===

Binary sampling (presence/absence) is frequently used where it is difficult to obtain accurate counts. The dispersal index (''D'') is used when the study population is divided into a series of equal samples ( number of units = ''N'': number of units per sample = ''n'': total population size = ''n'' x ''N'' ).<ref name=Gottwald2007>{{cite journal | last1 = Gottwald | first1 = TR | last2 = Bassanezi | first2 = RB | last3 = Amorim | first3 = L | last4 = Bergamin-Filho | first4 = A | year = 2007 | title = Spatial pattern analysis of citrus canker-infected plantings in São Paulo, Brazil, and augmentation of infection elicited by the Asian leafminer | journal = Phytopathology | volume = 97 | issue = 6| pages = 674–683 | doi=10.1094/phyto-97-6-0674| pmid = 18943598 | doi-access =}}</ref> The theoretical variance of a sample from a population with a binomial distribution is

: <math> s^2 = n p ( 1 - p ) </math>

where ''s''<sup>2</sup> is the variance, ''n'' is the number of units sampled and ''p'' is the mean proportion of sampling units with at least one individual present. The dispersal index (''D'') is defined as the ratio of observed variance to the expected variance. In symbols

: <math> D = \frac {\text{var}_\text{obs} } { \text{var}_\text{bin} } = \frac{s^2} {np(1 - p)}</math>

where var<sub>obs</sub> is the observed variance and var<sub>bin</sub> is the expected variance. The expected variance is calculated with the overall mean of the population. Values of ''D'' > 1 are considered to suggest aggregation. ''D''( ''n'' − 1 ) is distributed as the chi squared variable with ''n'' − 1 degrees of freedom where ''n'' is the number of units sampled.

An alternative test is the ''C'' test.<ref name=Hughes1993>{{cite journal | last1 = Hughes | first1 = G | last2 = Madden | first2 = LV | year = 1993 | title = Using the beta-binomial distribution to describe aggregated patterns of disease incidence | journal = Phytopathology | volume = 83 | issue = 9| pages = 759–763 | doi=10.1094/phyto-83-759}}</ref>

: <math> C = \frac { D( n N - 1 ) - n N } { ( 2 N (n^2 - n))^{1/2} } </math>

where ''D'' is the dispersal index, ''n'' is the number of units per sample and ''N'' is the number of samples. C is distributed normally. A statistically significant value of C indicates [[overdispersion]] of the population.

''D'' is also related to [[intraclass correlation]] (''ρ'') which is defined as<ref name=Fleiss1981>Fleiss JL (1981) Statistical methods for rates and proportions. 2nd ed. Wiley, New York, USA</ref>

: <math> \rho = 1 - \frac{ \sum x_i ( T - x_i ) } { p ( 1 - p ) N T ( T - 1 ) } </math>

where ''T'' is the number of organisms per sample, ''p'' is the likelihood of the organism having the sought after property (diseased, pest free, ''etc''), and x<sub>i</sub> is the number of organism in the ''i''th unit with this property. ''T'' must be the same for all sampled units. In this case with ''n'' constant

: <math> \rho = \frac{ D - 1 } { n - 1 } </math>

If the data can be fitted with a [[beta-binomial distribution]] then<ref name="Fleiss1981"/>

: <math> D = 1 + \frac{ (n - 1) \theta }{ 1 + \theta } </math>

where ''θ'' is the parameter of the distribution.<ref name=Hughes1993 />

===Ma's population aggregation critical density===

Ma has proposed a parameter (''m''<sub>0</sub>) − the population aggregation critical density - to relate population density to Taylor's law.<ref name=Ma1991>Ma ZS (1991) Further interpreted Taylor's Power Law and population aggregation critical density. Trans Ecol Soc China (1991) 284–288</ref>

: <math> m_0 = \exp\left( \frac{\log a}{1 - b} \right) </math>

==Related statistics==

A number of statistical tests are known that may be of use in applications.

===de Oliveria's statistic===

A related statistic suggested by de Oliveria<ref name=deOliveria1965>de Oliveria T (1965) Some elementary tests for mixtures of discrete distributions, ''in'' Patil, GP ''ed.'', Classical and contagious discrete distributions. Calcutá, Calcutta Publishing Society pp379-384</ref> is the difference of the variance and the mean.<ref name=Bohning1994>{{cite journal | last1 = Bohning | first1 = D | year = 1994 | title = A note on a test for Poisson overdispersion | journal =   Biometrika| volume = 81 | issue = 2| pages = 418–419 | doi=10.2307/2336974| jstor = 2336974 }}</ref> If the population is Poisson distributed then

: <math> var( s^2 - m ) = \frac{ 2t^2 } { n - 1 } </math>

where ''t'' is the Poisson parameter, ''s''<sup>2</sup> is the variance, ''m'' is the mean and ''n'' is the sample size. The expected value of ''s''<sup>2</sup> - ''m'' is zero. This statistic is distributed normally.<ref name=Ping1995>{{cite journal | last1 = Ping | first1 = S | year = 1995 | title = Further study on the statistical test to detect spatial pattern | journal =   Biometrical Journal| volume = 37 | issue = 2| pages = 199–203 | doi=10.1002/bimj.4710370211}}</ref>

If the Poisson parameter in this equation is estimated by putting ''t'' = ''m'', after a little manipulation this statistic can be written

: <math> O_T = \sqrt { \frac { n - 1 } { 2 } } \frac { s^2 - m } { m } </math>

This is almost identical to Katz's statistic with ( ''n'' - 1 ) replacing ''n''. Again ''O''<sub>''T''</sub> is normally distributed with mean 0 and unit variance for large ''n''. This statistic is the same as the Neyman-Scott statistic.

;Note

de Oliveria actually suggested that the variance of ''s''<sup>2</sup> - ''m'' was ( 1 - 2''t''<sup>1/2</sup> + 3''t'' ) / ''n'' where ''t'' is the Poisson parameter. He suggested that ''t'' could be estimated by putting it equal to the mean (''m'') of the sample. Further investigation by Bohning<ref name="Bohning1994"/> showed that this estimate of the variance was incorrect. Bohning's correction is given in the equations above.

===Clapham's test===

In 1936 Clapham proposed using the ratio of the variance to the mean as a test statistic (the relative variance).<ref name=Clapham1936>{{cite journal | last1 = Clapham | first1 = AR | year = 1936 | title = Overdispersion in grassland communities and the use of statistical methods in plant ecology | journal =  Journal of Ecology| volume = 14 | issue = 1| pages = 232–251 | doi = 10.2307/2256277 | jstor = 2256277 | bibcode = 1936JEcol..24..232C }}</ref> In symbols

: <math> \theta = \frac{ s^2 }{ m } </math>

For a Possion distribution this ratio equals 1. To test for deviations from this value he proposed testing its value against the chi square distribution with ''n'' degrees of freedom where ''n'' is the number of sample units. The distribution of this statistic was studied further by Blackman<ref name=Blackman1942>Blackman GE (1942) Statistical and ecological studies on the distribution of species in plant communities. I. Dispersion as a factor in the study of changes in plant populations. Ann Bot N.s. vi: 351</ref> who noted that it was approximately normally distributed with a mean of 1 and a variance ( ''V''<sub>θ</sub> ) of

: <math> V_{ \theta } = \frac{ 2n } { ( n - 1 )^2 } </math>

The derivation of the variance was re analysed by Bartlett<ref name=Greig-Smith1952>{{cite journal | last1 = Greig-Smith | first1 = P | year = 1952 | title = The use of random and contiguous quadrats in the study of the structure of plant communities | journal = Annals of Botany| volume = 16 | issue = 2| pages = 293–316 | doi=10.1093/oxfordjournals.aob.a083317}}</ref> who considered it to be

: <math> V_\theta = \frac 2 { n - 1 } </math>

For large samples these two formulae are in approximate agreement. This test is related to the later Katz's ''J''<sub>''n''</sub> statistic.

If the population obeys Taylor's law then

: <math> \theta = am^{b - 1} </math>

;Note

A refinement on this test has also been published<ref name=Gosset1986>{{cite journal | last1 = Gosset | first1 = E | last2 = Louis | first2 = B | year = 1986 | title = The binning analysis - Towards a better significance test | journal = Astrophysics and Space Science| volume = 120 | issue = 2| pages = 263–306 | bibcode = 1986Ap&SS.120..263G | doi = 10.1007/BF00649941 | hdl = 2268/88597 | s2cid = 117653758 | hdl-access = free }}</ref> These authors noted that the original test tends to detect overdispersion at higher scales even when this was not present in the data. They noted that the use of the multinomial distribution may be more appropriate than the use of a Poisson distribution for such data. The statistic ''θ'' is distributed

: <math> \theta = \frac{s^2} m = \frac 1 n \sum \left( x_i - \frac n N \right)^2 </math>

where ''N'' is the number of sample units, ''n'' is the total number of samples examined and ''x''<sub>i</sub> are the individual data values.

The expectation and variance of ''θ'' are

: <math> \operatorname E( \theta ) = \frac N { N - 1} </math>

: <math> \operatorname{Var}(\theta) = \frac{( N - 1 )^2} {N^3} - \frac {2N - 3} {nN^2}</math>

For large ''N'', E(''θ'') is approximately 1 and

: <math> \operatorname{Var}(\theta) \sim\ \frac 2 N \left( 1 - \frac 1 n \right) </math>

If the number of individuals sampled (''n'') is large this estimate of the variance is in agreement with those derived earlier. However, for smaller samples these latter estimates are more precise and should be used.
